title: Lost in Context: Adressing Context Anxiety in Large Language Models
claim: A failure mode driven by miscalibrated self-estimation harms accuracy and efficiency, but training on traces without it recovers performance.
layout: 2 stacked panels: three paired horizontal bars above, grouped vertical bars below
description: The figure has two stacked panels of bar charts, each with a caption below it. Panel (a), titled 'Impact of Context Anxiety', has three horizontal bar charts. Each compares 'Without Anxiety' (blue) with 'With Anxiety' (orange), and each carries a '***' significance marker. The top chart shows mean token ratio (0.81 vs 1.24). The middle chart shows task accuracy (67.5% vs 52.8%). The bottom chart shows mean completion tokens (4,317 vs 6,638). Panel (b), titled 'Reasoning Fine-Tuning Results', is a grouped vertical bar chart of accuracy. It covers Tower of Hanoi (3, 5 and 7 disks) and Shortest Path (5x5, 7x7 and 9x9 grids). Bars are Baseline (dark gray), Without Anxiety (blue) and All Correct (orange), with value labels above them. The eye goes first to the contrasting blue and orange bars in the top chart.
caption: Context anxiety stems from miscalibrated token estimation and creates a reduction in performance and efficiency (a), but context anxiety can be reduced through supervised fine tuning on reasoning traces without anxiety (b).
abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that reasoning models fail when problems exceed their capabilities. However, we find that frontier reasoning models sometimes possess the necessary capabilities to solve problems but fail due to premature self-doubt -- a phenomenon informally known as context anxiety. We provide the first systematic study of context anxiety, demonstrating that it arises, in part, from a model's inability to accurately estimate the tokens required to complete a task. We also show that context anxiety leads to material efficiency losses when models operate under perceived constraints. Building on this analysis, we further show that models can learn alternative strategies for solving long-horizon problems without exhibiting context anxiety, suggesting that performance improvements may be achievable not through scaling model capabilities, but by improving models' ability to accurately assess and adapt to their own limitations.
